The study reveals distinct behaviors between uniformly and non-uniformly expanding dynamical systems, as well as a crucial role played by preimages in correlation decay. Through a practical example, it is demonstrated that the preimages' structure in non-uniformly expanding systems can lead to recurring patterns in the transfer operator's eigenfunctions, causing correlation decay to occur at varying rates among different pairs of eigenfunctions, and in turn, giving rise to a mesoscopic-scale observed at an approximate scale of $\log(1+\lambda)$, where $\lambda$ represents the growth rate of the system, and'mesoscopic' in this context refers to an intermediate scale situated between microscopic and macroscopic ones.

A general covering array with parameters (q, n, t, L) is said to be constructed if its rows can cover all possible t-fold combinations of the set {1, 2,..., q} at least once within every subset L of {1, 2,..., n}.  A special type of general covering array, defined by specific subset structure of L, is referred to as a uniform covering array.  Covering array strength, represented by the minimum size of L, determines the efficiency of this combinatorial design.  Researchers have been working on reducing the size of general covering arrays, previously studied under the name uniform, to better perform in comparison.  This study aims to develop an algorithm for determining an optimal general covering array, based on a given parameter set (q, n, t, L), and further investigate properties of the resulting combinatorial design.  Additionally, a detailed analysis of the characteristics of the previously studied uniform covering arrays will be conducted based on their known properties.  This analysis will provide insight into the covering array's generalization potential.  An evaluation of the proposed algorithm's computational efficiency will also be conducted.  This study's time complexity analysis reveals that solving the general covering array problem becomes more computationally intensive as the size of the set q increases, but remains relatively efficient for small values of q.  In contrast, the size of the set L has minimal impact on the algorithm's computational demands.  An additional advantage of the proposed

We examine the impact of quantum resource sharing on the quantum advantage in a two-player game using copies of a bipartite state. Our analysis reveals that having access to multiple instances of a state can enhance the strategic player's chances, as shared quantum resources can facilitate predicting the other player's measurement outcomes earlier. A shared pair of qubits suffices to achieve an unbeatable strategy, however our computations reveal that sharing N states yields an increased winning probability only when N is less than a threshold value, specifically less than the logarithm of N to the base 2.5. The strategic value of having extra states becomes apparent when considering the strategic value which increases linearly with N, while the required computational resources for solving the problem grow exponentially with N.

Artificial intelligence can improve software safety by analyzing the causes of program crashes.  Previous models, such as EvoCrash, used evolutionary learning to discover changes leading to crashes in other programs.  However, our test cases suggest that EvoCrash may have overlooked direct modifications causing crashes and instead focused on random changes that result in program crashes.  This random scenario can make it difficult for EvoCrash to accurately predict crash causes.  To verify the effectiveness of EvoCrash, we created new test cases that directly modify crash-causing coding elements and found that EvoCrash frequently fails to pinpoint the causal mutation when there's a direct modification present.  On the other hand, our study shows that EvoCrash can effectively identify random changes that result in program crashes on other programs, such as those that involve input-annotated coding elements.  Consequently, we recommend using EvoCrash for predicting random crashes that involve these coding elements, as long as there's no direct modification causing the crash.  Ultimately, our research indicates that more advanced AI techniques, such as fine-tuned neural networks, are necessary for accurately discovering direct modifications causing program crashes.

In an anisotropic $d$-wave superconductor, a finite quasiparticle gap modulates the Fermi surface, forming multiple distinct periods. As a result, the lattice of vortices undergoes a transitional phase change similar to a solid to liquid phase transition, with the number of phases equaling the number of periods. Utilizing an extended theory combining the Pomeranchuk and rotational transitions, the present study explores the lattice of vortices in $d$-wave superconductors and identifies parameters yielding an irregular and disordered phase arrangement. Comparing these results with symmetry-related symmetry classes in three-dimensional systems, the present research reconciles disparate theoretical predictions and experimental outcomes. Specifically, the present research addresses and resolves a long-standing controversy concerning whether the lattice of vortices in $YBa_2CuO_{4+\delta}$ undergoes an irregular disordering as it is rotated.

Using the EPOS3 event generator, we have carried out simulations to model the development of collective flow in high-energy heavy ion collisions. By analyzing the EPOS3 simulations, we have found a direct relationship between the spatial distribution of final particles and the flow coefficients in the transverse plane. Based on these findings, we have developed a method to quantify the ratio of v_2 to v_3 coefficients in both the EPOS3 model and simulated proton-proton collisions. By comparing the results to theoretical predictions obtained from ideal fluid dynamics, we have found that this ratio can serve as a indicator of the complex, multi-component nature of the quark-gluon plasma state. Furthermore, we have shown that this approach enables us to extract information on the QGP's initial conditions, serving as a sensitive test for both the EPOS3 model and theoretical models of fluid dynamics.

Using exact diagonalization, we have found the wave patterns in triangular and kagome structures when subjected to an in-plane magnetic field, both with and without flux. Our findings show that certain spin configurations exhibit unexpected connections between energy and spin, as well as between magnetic and crystal structures. Specifically, we have identified two unique wave patterns that can be controlled by adjusting the field and flux, and may be linked to rare magnetic orders. We also discovered that merging rare magnetic orders can host unusual magnetic patterns, and that applying an out-of-plane field can trigger a shift from long-range to short-range ordering, and even lead to no ordering at all within a certain temperature range.

This research introduces two statistical methods that combine similarity between patients and propensity scores to enhance the statistical power of identifying an overall treatment effect, while maintaining an acceptable false discovery rate in multiple testing situations. The two methods are facilitated by previous findings that overlapping propensity scores among similar patients exhibit underwriting a Q-statistic, which effectively captures treatment response commonality. The first method builds upon the idea of controlling the false discovery rate through inductive inference, utilising categorical score distributions to establish p-values for treatment effectiveness. The second method leverages the fact that logarithmic p-values are normally distributed, allowing the calculation of q-values by approximating normal distribution-based score distributions. In both cases, the aim is to determine the minimum significance level required to maintain an acceptable false discovery rate, making better use of similarity information to enhance overall treatment effect detection power. This research also incorporates simulation datasets in size-exponential series, as well as real-world data from the CTCAE 3.0 adjuvant chemotherapy trial for treating non-small cell lung cancer and triple-negative breast cancer treatments to validate the proposed methods.

The Large Synoptic Survey Camera (LSBC) on the LSST's 10m telescope at Cerro Panchito will study the sky with a 10 square degree field of view. It will use a series of 10 image stacks per night, building to 30 image stacks by the end of the project in 2026. By combining the stacks in time domain, scientists will be able to track changes in the movement and brightness of objects in the sky. By combining the sets 300 times, scientists will be able to look at objects in the very early universe. TheLSBC will study the movement and brightness of objects in the early universe by combining the sets 300 times, and its precise images will be available through a dataset called the LSBC Drift Scan dataset. TheLSBC Drift Scan dataset will be available at the LSST Data Management website. In the early universe, theLSBC will be able to detect changes in the temperature fluctuations in the very early universe. The precise images in theLSBC Drift Scan dataset will be available in the near-ir spectrum, and will be used to determine the wave length of the temperature fluctuations in the very early universe. By combining the results with simulations of the universe, scientists will be able to determine the parameters of the very early universe's inflationary period. TheLSBC will be able to detect changes in the very early universe's polarization, and will be one of the first instruments to study this effect. The

A recent analysis of the Higgs boson decays at the Large Hadron Collider reveals signs of a larger self-coupling of the Higgs field than expected within the Standard Model. Additionally, discrepancies in the muon's magnetic moment and W boson mass, observed before the LHC era, can be resolved within a two Higgs doublet model featuring non-minimal Yukawa interactions. By incorporating these observations into a global fit, a type-X two Higgs doublet model emerges as the most plausible explanation. However, the same model is constrained by its failure to explain an excess of like-sign lepton events observed in the Tevatron experiment. A synthetic scenario is created by combining all constraints, excluding only the anomalous signal in the muon's magnetic moment and the Higgs self-coupling for type-X two Higgs doublet model predictions. As a result, a synthetic scenario arises, where the Higgs self-coupling is significantly larger than Standard Model expectations, even when considering LHC data at its current stage.

Software project managers face challenges Crowdsourcing concept location efforts to speed up development. Although crowdsourcing has been successfully applied to various software engineering tasks, integrating concept location with crowdsourcing remains an underutilized area. Our research investigates concept location crowdsourcing through the context of label definition identification. In this study, we introduce two crowdsourcing approaches: (1) Guided Crowdsourcing, which provides developers with general concept information, and (2) Augmented Guided Crowdsourcing, which pre-filters potential answers. Our experimental results show that both approaches are viable, our experiments were conducted using the JMeter platform and consisted of 90 software projects. Our results, based on the evaluation of 189 tasks by 29 experienced programmers, demonstrate that Augmented Guided Crowdsourcing outperforms Guided Crowdsourcing by 10% in accuracy but there is no significant difference in their efficiency. Our research demonstrates that crowdsourcing can be a valuable alternative to traditional concept location methods, enabling the use of more natural and unstructured general concept information. Our study also explores the optimal number of task distributors and general concept statements. Our results demonstrate that using 3 distributors and 3 general concept statements yields the best performance, improving efficiency by 13.6% and 21.9% respectively.

Conversational distance metrics have been applied to assess the authenticity of conversations between human pairs. The goal is to determine whether the distance metric can identify unauthentic, manually fabricated conversations distinct from genuine conversations. This study employs the Neural Entrainment Distance (NED) measure, a statistical analysis of linguistic patterns that reflects the degree of conversational coordination between speakers. Previous research indicated that NED can pinpoint fabricated conversations. This study investigates whether incorporating contextual aspects can enhance the NED metric in differentiating authentic from unauthentic conversations. The results show that incorporating context fails to substantially improve the NED metric in differentiating authentic from unauthentic conversations.

We utilize the predicted line emission from the P18 galaxy simulation to evaluate BPT diagnostic plots. Employing the same analysis methods used for observational data, we obtain detailed reports for each galaxy, including a comprehensive list of diagnostic results and a classification into distinct emission line categories. These classifications are compared to the simulated star formation classifications. Although the predicted emission contains numerous observed ions, some lines (such as [O III] 88um) are not present in the simulations. A lack of specific data from extreme emission or absorption is thought to contribute to this absence. Nonetheless, the presence of [O III] 500um is accurately predicted. Our findings indicate that, when viewed from close range, the simulated spectra fail to distinguish the dominant processes creating the emission. However, this distinction becomes apparent at closer stellar environments. The spectra of younger than 10 million-year stars and supernova-creating regions show clear differences, whereas the spectra of older stars are generally inconspicuous. The diagrams accurately classify star-forming galaxies with star formation rates exceeding 1 Msun per year about 70% of the time but struggle with identifying galaxies powered solely by active galactic nuclei.

Action recognition research has focused on classification over action detection, despite the latter being more challenging. To address this disparity, we introduce the Co-occurrence Action Parsing (CAP) framework for predicting accurate and detailed action detection data. CAP achieves this through an innovative parsing module that leverages co-occurrence information. By employing a advanced action detection dataset that combines video temporal segmentation and annotated atomic actions, we evaluate CAP and show significant enhancements over existing methods in multiple metrics. Furthermore, we note that CAP generalizes well to other evaluation tasks, including top-down classification, bottom-up action detection, and action recognition. Through cap-densecap, we also demonstrate significant advancements in action detection benchmarks, surpassing the state-of-the-art. Our work lays the groundwork for an action recognition pipeline that addresses both top-down and bottom-up tasks in the future.

We analyze the most extensive data set from the LHCb experiment for the $ \Lambda_b^0$ particle's exclusive two-body decays into final states including $J/\psi$, $D^0$, $D^+$, and $K^-$ particles. Utilizing a relative production rate interpretation, we examine the angular distributions of particles at decay points using a model that accounts for long-lived particles, linear polarization, and decay orientations. This analysis is the first to measure linear polarization parameters for specific decay modes: $\Lambda_b^0 \rightarrow J/\psi p K^-$, $\Lambda_b^0 \rightarrow D^0 K^-$, and $\Lambda_b^0 \rightarrow D^+ K^-$.

We evaluated the effect of two algorithms that determine provided feedback to students in a online testing and grading setting. Twenty-four students received either general assistance or personalized feedback along with their course materials. Their performance was compared to those who received no additional feedback. Eighteen students participated in a study where their testing and grading history showed improved code coverage and enhanced grades for eleven of the students who received feedback, with improvements ranging from 8% to 23%. Those who received general feedback performed similarly to those who received personalized feedback, suggesting that any form of support is more effective than offering none. Our research indicates that automated feedback is an economical solution for improving student outcomes.

Unquarantine, a newly proposed framework, enables domain adaptation without relying on target-domain source data, thereby overcoming the limitations typically encountered in traditional methods. To circumvent the absence of target data, Unquarantine incorporates an unsupervised target classifier into a source-data-only trainer, using a novel training strategy based on dual propagation networks to resolve this issue. Specifically, it employs a source-data classifier, a target-data predictor, and a balance regulator to create an robust and generalizable target classifier. As an explicit step, it introduces an optional target classifier using an entropy-maximizing strategy based on Negative Auxiliary Loss for handling situations where sources are labeled, while using an implicit target classifier, an ERM-maximizing strategy based on Negative Auxiliary Loss, when sources are unlabeled. Importantly, the target classifier's contributions are adjustable via an auto-mutual information approach, thereby allowing the selection of most relevant source data for replication and target prediction. Our comprehensive evaluations of Unquarantine have been performed on seven benchmark datasets from diverse domains, including prosthetic vision, acoustic noise-robustness, and multi-sensory learning, thereby testing its generalizability and robustness. The experimental outcomes demonstrate Unquarantine's capabilities to achieve a high target domain performance even in extreme situations, such as source data corruption, excess, and scarcity, while outperforming state-of-the-art adaptation methods in most cases. Our research findings suggest that Unquarantine's source-data-only

The primary objective of this research is to develop a detailed prediction tool that can be applied across various fuel types and core designs. The focus of this work lies in predicting the thermal behavior of a gas core reactor, which is an internal fluid-fuel reactor featuring directly heated gas rods within a stainless steel container. The proposed prediction tool employs established models from the literature to model thermal behavior. The prediction tool was initially tested for consistency by comparing it's predictions with experimental data from the GCR experiment conducted by the Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The prediction tool was used to simulate and study the effect of pressure and number of gas rods on the operating temperature and power output of a gas core reactor. The results show that the prediction tool can accurately simulate the outcome of a test facility, highlighting the significance of pressure and fuel amount on the operation of a gas core reactor. The study further reveals that the operation of a gas core reactor can switch between convective and radiative heat transfer, depending on pressure and core design. The prediction tool is recommended as a preliminary design aid to facilitate comparison between different design options. Further research is required to validate the use of established models for advanced fuel applications.

We suggest incorporating topological information from particle detectors into neural networks by using a special function that amounts to a weighted mixture of local momenta. This novel neural network architecture, which combines prior knowledge of detectors with pure neural modeling, demonstrates topological merit and is useful for general machine learning tasks in particle physics. By using placeholder variables for missing data, our network can handle missing information, making it versatile and applicable to a broad range of problems. Unlike earlier models, our network does not require redefining variables for training and can maintain its original variable structure, though variable standardization is recommended for better performance. We have tested the network's efficacy on two specific problems: identifying isolated electrons and identifying long-lived proposed LHCb charm mesons known as $Q_2^*$.

Specifically, our network achieved an isolation efficiency of about 98.5% for electrons with pseudorapidity $|η| < 2.0$ and efficiency better than other competing models. Moreover, our architecture achieved a remarkable $97.5\%$ purity in identifying $Q_2^{*}$ decays with specific topological characteristics, outperforming its competitors by a margin of about 3%. These results demonstrate the potential of our network as a powerful tool for addressing a wide array of particle physics data analysis challenges.

In simulations of extremely hot Jupiter-like planets and red dwarf stars, our model's accuracy is tested by analyzing the impact of excitation action lists for titanium oxide emissions. Our study sets bounds on usable TiO emission lists depending on atmospheric temperature. In models of MDWarfs with TiO present, we discover shorter possible lists compared to those in planets with TiO present. These lists, ranging from 50 to 150 lines, are contingent upon temperature and pressure levels. Extending beyond these bounds results in minimal impact on model output. In planets with TiO, reduced line options yield decreased irradiated companion temperature. In stars with TiO, reduced line options yield a notable 10K decrease in equilibrium temperature. Our research demonstrates varying influence of TiO emissions depending on whether we're analyzing a gaseous planet or a solid star. Furthermore, our models of N4U1738140 also reveal that using high-resolution spectra involving over 3000 lines (as in the SETI Institute's model), resulting in increased pressure, leads to negligible differences compared to observed data. Our observations indicate that models of ultra-hot subjects are insensitive to the composition of computational TiO line lists, provided that the total line count remains below 150K.

This publication examines the computational characteristics of Answer Set Programming (ASP) in handling indeterminate logic programs featuring nested collective aggregates. We expand on the existing ASP semantics to formally define the semantics of collectively aggregated goals. Furthermore, this paper outlines the computational limitations associated with handling nested collective aggregates using standard ASP resolution, demonstrating that the problem often becomes inherently complex (undecidable). To address this challenge, we also introduce an advanced grounding algorithm designed for logic programs with nested collective aggregates that translates these goals into extended clause-language rules during the grounding process. In contrast to ASP resolution, our proposed method ensures decidability in such scenarios.

A unified framework is developed to express the second law of thermodynamics for a general set of systems with multiple resources. The concept of state transformation is extended beyond entropy increases alone, and it mathematically proves that certain combinations of resource attributes cannot decrease. The ideas are applied to thermodynamic value flows in electrical circuits and thermal systems, and it's shown that the principles underlying conservation laws also imply the second law of thermodynamics. The underlying theories studied include multi-component theories, theories based on hierarchically connected attributes, and those where attributes interact in complex ways.

We introduce a new approach to estimating mutual information by utilizing the moments of random variables. A set of unbiased moment estimators is derived for mutual information, min-entropy, and max-entropy, which can be calculated using a centralized or distributed computation. The stability of these estimators is evaluated in terms of their bias and variance, with the requirement that their variance diminishes as the sample size increases. Moreover, it is demonstrated how to calculate the parameters of a parametric distribution (such as the Gaussian distribution) based on the moments of its components. Our methodology is substantiated through various numerical experiments, which demonstrate its efficacy in estimating information measures when only limited data is available.

This research proposes and evaluates a new estimator for the number of common stochastic trends in a multivariate time series, using a Lagrange Multiplier test based on the Linear Factor Model. The estimator achieves consistent results even when dealing with heavy-tailed distributions and changes in sample size. In finite samples, it exhibits asymptotic normality. The investigator conducts a Monte Carlo simulation to examine the estimator's reliability across various scenarios and real-world examples. The results show that the proposed estimator performs well and surpasses existing competitors under heavy-tailed conditions. Furthermore, an application to the S&P500 index returns demonstrates that the proposed approach can detect the existence of common stochastic trends and isolate random components, even when short-lived.

Quantum codes constructed using the Cayley complex are highly efficient due to their
high threshold capabilities. We focus on developing a framework for creating these codes
from a specific class of groups with a high degree of variability. By systematically
generating the complex and identifying its key structures, we obtain narrow quantum codes
with significant code rates. Moreover, our method allows us to obtain the minimum distance
of the code and determine whether it is optimal. We also present some exemplary codes
derived from the symmetric group.

We analyze the fundamental data structure, known as Independent Set, within the context of distributed computation on graph types, specifically, $r$-dominating sets in graphs where every vertex has at least four connections. This problem is further explored under a specific framework, and our research demonstrates the feasibility of an approximate solution using minimum $r$-dominating set algorithms. By applying this approach, we achieve two significant results - a linear-time algorithm capable of finding a 2-approximate solution in tree-like structures, and a similar 2-approximate solution with the same linear-time efficiency in bipartite graph types, where every vertex is connected to at least four other vertices.

Numerical investigations were conducted to assess the impact of disorder on higher-order topological insulators, with a focus on a model consisting of 2D, 3D, and 2.5-dimensional lattice structures. Using the Peierls substitution, we introduced disorder into the Hubbard model, which was then expanded into different spatial dimensions via the inverse transformation of a vector potential. Following this, we calculated the disorder-induced changes to bulk and boundary gaps within a one-dimensional ribbon extracted from the model. Our main conclusion is that the influence of disorder on the gaps at the boundary significantly outperforms its impact on the gaps in the bulk in cases of topological insulators of order $n\geq 2$. This phenomenon can be attributed to the inherent nature of the boundary in naturally amplifying disorder-induced fluctuations. Moreover, we observed that the boundary can effectively counteract the effects of disorder that is randomly applied in higher-order topical insulators, with a disorder strength of randomly applied electrons of approximately $0.1t$, where $t$ designates the nearest-neighbor hopping, except for the case of a two-dimensional topological insulator at finite temperature.

Using data collected from 2016 proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, which total 36.3 fb$^{-1}$, a search for highly compressed, long-lived charginos that decay into photons and electrons or muons was performed. The analysis focused on rare final states with photons in the electron and muon detectors, and on muons associated with significant energy dissipation due to the track's high momentum. No difference was found beyond the standard model's expected results. In the searched scenarios, a chargino mass constraint, initially assuming it decays at the electron-electron collider, was used. Constraints were established on the production of charginos with lifetimes ranging from 10 ns to almost 100 ns, which is at least an order of magnitude more strict than what was seen before, specifically when the chargino mass is around 500 GeV. Also, another set of constraints was established, which involved photons in the detectors and assumed that the chargino mass is roughly half that of the neutralino's mass. Ultimately, the searched data revealed compressed, long-lived chargino masses starting at around 350 GeV, with a 3.8 TeV upper bound, assuming that the chargino decays at the electron-electron collider; these results match what was seen before in the searched data.

Our approach, DeepLF, uses deep learning to reconstruct a full 3D scene from only a few views, employing a geometric constraint to enhance the accuracy of its self-supervised training. DeepLF leverages geometric formulas to calculate the distance between its generated views and the actual scene, thereby regulating its performance through geometric precision. As new data becomes available, it adapts its representation of scene geometry to fit its new knowledge, leading to the improvement of its overall performance. DeepLF's ability to combine geometric constraints with its flexible neural representation yields superior reconstruction of complex 3D geometry, particularly in the case of multiple objects and intricate scenes, as evidenced by its performance on the NLRF dataset.

Our speckle interferometric study at the SOAR observatory covered a six-year time frame from 2014 to 2020, focusing on a significant subset of nearby star systems. Under ideal seeing and telescope conditions, we conducted high-precision observations at various P.I. seeing conditions. A total of 60 star systems were examined, out of which we identified new binary or multi-body companions in 14 systems, along with an additional 17 existing known sub-systems within these systems' neighborhoods. Furthermore, our research expanded the knowledge of the TW Hydrae group by discovering a new companion, and a nearby star was found to be potentially associated with the Sirius group, marked by the presence of a new speckle detectable binary system. These findings were verified using Doppler radial velocity detection methods and subsequently published in a separate study. Moreover, our research aided in grading GJ 729's tertiary companion using astrometric analysis and constrained the mass ratio of its putative primary component. We examined Speckle Detectable Binary Detections' astrometric and color-index magnitudes, and based on these, we inferred plausible mass estimations for the tertiary companion.

In chiral conformal field theories, we investigate the structure of the operator-product expansion (OPE) with respect to the symmetry $\mathfrak{m}$. Our work focuses on self-dual models where the OPE's associativity properties can be directly probed using the $ad$-admissibility condition, revealing a unique relationship between chiral OPEs and scattering amplitudes. Furthermore, we establish the condition of $ad$-admissibility as the mathematical framework for an extension of the OPE, capable of addressing cases with non-trivial S-matrix elements.

A newly identified solar jet has been discovered using the Haleakala Solar Telescope's adaptive optics system, moving at 76 km/s and exhibiting root-mean-square (rms) enhancements of 150 km/s. Analyzing a type II radio burst, we calculated the shock speed to be 156 km/s and found it might be accelerated by a solar jet similar to the one observed. Furthermore, we suggest that one possible mechanism driving the shock acceleration could be the jet interacting with an underlying magnetic field, causing it to steepen and generate the observed type II radio burst through a scenario such as the "forward shock" or "termination shock." Finally, we speculate that the solar jet observed could be part of a circular band drifting towards the north pole. If the structure were located at mid-latitudes, its height would be approximately 20-30 Mm, although at higher mid-latitude locations, such a model becomes increasingly speculative.

Using a global $\chi^2$ fit, we investigated how various observables in B meson decays and collider experiments fit together. Our analysis was based on a particular model, called the 2HDM, which so far has shown the best ability to explain past experimental results. We focused on 8 and 13 TeV data from LHC, as well as future plans for P2, BEPCII, and ILC, in addition to other past experiments. We found that, if the model is correct, we should see certain changes at upcoming facilities. These potential breakthroughs could help us better understand the underlying physics behind the behavior of leptons, in particular, electron-positron interactions, which could potentially be beyond the Standard Model.

We introduce a novel numerical approach that uses a dynamic streamfunction formulation
for solving three-dimensional incompressible fluid flow equations on the
commutative lattice structure. This approach combines the benefits of the fast Fourier transform
with the versatility of the lattice Boltzmann method. Interpolating the streamfunction over
interlaced grid levels creates localized vortices which are set to zero and then allowed to
evolve according to a specific set of rules. This evolution results in enhanced transport properties
and a significant reduction or elimination of unnecessary phase volumes. By further optimizing
the phase volume removal process and incorporating fast Poisson solver techniques, it is possible
to significantly accelerate simulations on a commutative lattice. This new method can be applied
to complex simulations such as turbulent flows, mixing dynamics, and droplet diffusion.
Additionally, it has the potential to significantly accelerate self-consistent lattice gauge simulations.

To analyze quantum information properties, we investigate the steady-state properties of a dynamically-generated GHZ toroidal chain, derived from the family of bosonic Gaussian chains. Utilizing exact lattice equations, we find that the Gaussian Gaussian theory replicates the exact Gaussian theory results. Notably, as the subsystem size approaches half the total number of photons, entanglement within the system reaches its maximum, as does variance. Moreover, as the subsystem size approaches a quarter of the total number of photons, entanglement essentially dies out. Additionally, as the subsystem size approaches half the total number of photons, purity reaches its maximum.

Our proposed Model Prune Relearn (MPR) pipeline effectively identifies the predictive variables needed to forecast future sample outcomes from large-scale time-sensitive genetic data. MPR seamlessly integrates Relevance Learning, dimensionality reduction, and feature selection to efficiently extract relevant information from complex data. By utilizing non-linear dimensionality reduction techniques to create a relevant umbrella manifold representation, MPR bypasses the limitations of linear algorithms. Its utility in studying multicellular organisms, such as individuals throughout a family, is demonstrated through applications in predictive variable identification, predictive model construction, and automated disease diagnosis. Moreover, MPR variants have been developed that specifically address prior knowledge, imbalanced data, and multiclass disease diagnoses. MPR's robustness and consistency across biological replicates and cross-platform analyses across different cellular types are substantiated by both synthetic and real-world examples.

In the field of control theory for complex systems that are difficult to measure, researchers use techniques like POMCP to simulate the actions of an optimal player, even when numerous state variables are uncertain and interconnected. This paper explores a connection between POMCP and recurrent neural networks, specifically focusing on how beliefs about system states converge to the network's hidden states. This equivalence serves as the basis for our main contribution, which is an algorithm that combines the strengths of RNNs and Monte-Carlo Tree Search to provide the most optimal actions, especially for complex systems that are difficult to model mathematically. This new algorithm has been tested and is effective at solving control problems that are easy to with standard methods, as well as systems that are considered extremely challenging due to high uncertainty about future system states, large possible actions, and large player memory. It is also able to learn faster when put into practice over many similar tasks, a feature known as transfer learning.

This paper addresses the action detection task in videos, using a combination of visual and language inputs. To capture the video's temporal context, the proposed method utilizes self-action for attention and then averages the attention values with frame features, feeding these into a Graph Convolutional Network. The network's predictive components include not only image-classification-like objects but also action-specific classes. Extensive testing on CARS196 and JFT300 datasets reveals that the proposed approach achieves an estimated 0.5 to 64% mAP increase over baseline methods, set aside for testing hyperparameters, when using JFT300 data compared to CARS300. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/yding61/GSM.

Most current deep learning-based techniques for image copy detection overlook
the underlying capabilities that allow many state-of-the-art approaches to
function.  A comprehensive survey of recent advances in this field reveals that
most successful methods utilize two essential components: a backbone network for
feature extraction and a matching algorithm that compares extracted features to
determine similarity.  This comprehensive literature review classifies existing image
copy detection approaches into several categories based on the task they
perform, and analyzes the development trends and shifts, highlighting the
advantages and drawbacks of each classification branch.  Furthermore, it analyzes
the impact of various deep learning architectures on image copy detection and
outlines several promising research directions for future development.

The analysis of linear stability in rotating shallow-water models has historically relied on idealized scenarios with homogeneous Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions. However, real-world applications involve complex coastal geometries necessitating general boundary conditions. Building on previous research, we develop a comprehensive theoretical framework for solving linearized Euler equations within these complex domains. Specifically, we develop initial-boundary value problems for domains with mixed boundary conditions, incorporating both interior and boundary resonances. Notably, we demonstrate that while our methods share core principles with existing homogeneous cases, explicit considerations are required for boundary resonances even with Dirichlet conditions, underscoring the importance of carefully constructed homogeneous boundary data.

Similar to nucleons, chiral edge states of fractional quantum Hall systems experience three key properties - they follow Dolan-Primakoff relations, exhibit energy and spin polarization in the absence of a magnetic field, and bind together when the magnetic field is set to zero. A key property of both nucleons and chiral edge states is the presence of angular momentum, which is also seen in the interactions between these states. When the magnetic field is set to zero, these states bind together. Furthermore, we have identified the forces behind interactions between two chiral edge states and suggestions for experimental verification of these findings are provided.

This paper explores an often-overlooked link between Differential Privacy and the lossy compression technique used in Federated Learning algorithms. We start by introducing a new framework, called DPk, that establishes a precise relationship between these algorithms and lossy compression techniques. Our framework is built on two key components: precise formulas describing data compression's effect on accuracy, and a definition of privacy in terms of compression distortion. We investigate the nature of DPk, applying it to binary classification problems where we identify a trade-off between accuracy and privacy, quantifiable in terms of compression distortion. Our study also sheds light on the interplay between data transmission efficiency, compression rate, and privacy levels.

Our research reveals UV images of over 2000 early-type stars within the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus star-forming complex. These images were derived from PIPODI-FP/SDFD data of approximately 170 all-sky UV images collected using the Sky-Map project's UV telescope. The data encompasses a specific wavelength range of roughly 300-3800 Angstroms. Our analysis shows that the combined far-ultraviolet intensity of over 1500 stars within the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus star-forming complex is a result of H2 fluorescent emission, and contributes roughly 60% of the total intensity. The remaining 40% is attributed to other sources such as late-type stars, and various astrophysical phenomena like supernovae, X-ray binary systems, radio galactic nuclei, and supernova remnants. Our analysis also indicates that within the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus star-forming complex, and adjacent areas, there are 33 newly identified early-type stars with far-ultraviolet emission, and a list of candidate deuterium-depleted early-type stars in the adjacent areas. These findings were also compared against data from other existing research sources, and newly identified candidates were also introduced. Our analysis further reveals the far-ultraviolet characteristics of SAGA-Gaia early-type stars within the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus star-forming complex, and adjacent areas, and further compares

We propose a novel two-stage method for extracting tables from document images. First, we utilize Graph Neural Networks to incorporate context and guide table detection, thereby identifying potential table cells. Subsequently, the predicted table cells are fed into a subsequent module for joint table recognition and structure prediction via a Conditional Random Field model, leveraging cells as joint prior and intermediate information to optimize the output. Our approach demonstrates the emergence of superior performance on the ICDAR 2019 Table and Table+Layout datasets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods by significant margins, with enhancements of 6.8% and 11.8% in table detection and reconstruction F1-score, respectively. Our project code is available online for public access.

In the Bugbrain Bugshow, a two-player zero-sum game involving sequential decision-making involving imperfect knowledge, we investigate how players make choices over numerous possible actions. Through the application of the belief Bayesian model, our findings indicate that higher-level learners discover a effective strategy early on, whereas lower-level learners may require multiple attempts to develop a effective approach. Notably, our results reveal that higher-level learners tend to generate fewer options in their decisions, reflecting a clearer understanding of 'face' configurations, as the level increases. The Bugshow also serves as a case study to assess the capabilities of the belief Bayesian model, an improvement over the traditional Bayesian model in situations characterized by changing action and state spaces.

This paper evaluates the effectiveness of network architecture design for a population
prediction task using crowd-sourced mapping and estimation techniques. By investigating
the potential of learning population patterns from informal data, we examined a dataset
of Facebook user account locations in Ghana. Our research involved comparing a traditional
approach using public attributes to a novel method utilizing estimated footprint area.
The findings show that incorporating estimated footprint area increases R-squared value by
20% and decreases Mean Squared Error by 123% compared to the public attribute alone.
Furthermore, we explored the feasibility of training a model using only crowd-sourced
mapping features, which suggests that learning population patterns from informal data is
promising. By incorporating estimated footprint area, we developed a model with 85% more
explanatory power than the traditional method. This research identifies key challenges in
working with crowd-sourced data, including the lack of formal data and potential bias.
Ultimately, our study paves the way for incorporating crowd-sourced data into demographic
estimation.

A proposed method for preventing the spread of false information on social media involves introducing a new type of filter. Unlike traditional filters that only aim to reduce shared content, the proposed system aims to achieve two main goals: minimizing the likelihood of false positives while minimizing the impact on system resources and speed. To accomplish this, the proposed method integrates the capabilities of social media analytics and machine learning to identify patterns in online behavior and predict potential cases of social media abuse. By leveraging this analysis, the system generates an adaptive hierarchy of filters that are tailored to individual users' online activities, resulting in a more effective and efficient approach to detecting and preventing social media abuse.

We develop a simplified model of a tightly bound atom-molecule system, utilizing a non-rigid pendulum framework, to analyze an intrinsic instability caused by an intrinsic loss process and explore its connection to a phenomenon known as an ergodic transition. By modifying the pendulum model to include a loss term representing the rate of change in the center-of-mass motion, it is observed that this loss can give rise to a rapid oscillating phenomenon. We apply a mean-field approximation to obtain a set of three coupled non-linear mean-field equations which can be rearranged into a modified non-linear resonator model. By analyzing this modified model, it is discovered that it shares a crucial characteristic with a real pendulum system, namely, instability. We present an analytical solution that illustrates the onset of this loss-induced instability and an examination using a time-evolving propagator approach, comparing these findings to experimental data obtained from radio-frequency spectra. Furthermore, it is observed that this loss-induced instability gives rise to a phenomenon known as an ergodic transition when viewed through the lens of a quantum ergodicity breakdown measure. Lastly, it is discovered that there are two distinct physical processes at play, described by two separate time-evolving behaviors, that can be accurately represented using the proposed model.

The Flexible Multi-Phase SPH Framework, incorporating a straightforward pseudo-pressure algorithm and a transport equation for phase fraction, forms the foundation of our model. This framework is designed to be compatible with any Single-Phase SPH method. Within our Multi-Phase SPH Framework, artificial voids are minimized through a dynamic initialization method that establishes a initial, random proper density for each particle, eliminating the need for previous Densification procedures. Furthermore, the FMPF can naturally resolve phase separation issues that may arise from differences in density ratios by maintaining stability even at first-order phase transition scenarios, eliminating the occurrence of negative mass errors and eliminating the need for artificial smooth lencth changes. As such, the FMPF, when integrated with Westenkov's mass distribution, can accurately predict the crystallization process of iron nucleated at the poles of spherical balls under gravity conditions without the artificial influences of cut-off distances and artificial viscosities.

A potential application of quantum computing lies in the clustering algorithm K-means. A quantum-based version of K-means has been developed, incorporating a quantum-based means of searching for data points closest to each other within the feature space. Research indicates that clustering can be accomplished in approximately O(epsilon^-2 * nd + k) time, with nd representing the dimensions of the data points and k the number of clusters, and epsilon a threshold value, in contrast to prior algorithms exhibiting asymptotic complexity of O(Nk).

Utilizing large speech datasets with standard prosodic characteristics can significantly
enhance speech synthesis models' ability to alter pitch. However, such datasets are
currently scarce to non-existent. Traditional methods for augmenting pitch datasets
involve shifting the fundamental frequency while maintaining frame independence.
Yet, in this study, our pitch-augmentation dataset does not alter the speaker's
identity and maintains the context's integrity by incorporating F0-driven retiming.
This data augmentation strategy significantly expands the possible pitch ranges in our
dataset without compromising its integrity. We observed that models trained on
pitch-augmented datasets produced synthesized speech with more natural pitch
variations when comparing them to models trained on unaltered datasets.

Objects within a scene are interconnected through relationships. Traditionally, models have focused either on individual objects within a scene or on the relationships they possess. To address this, our work introduces a dual-encoder framework where a scene is represented by an object-centric model and a relationship-centric model, respectively. To bridge the gap between these two models, we propose a training strategy based on contrastive learning to encourage the models to view the scene from a shared, object-centric perspective. By doing so, it allows the models to reason about objects in a scene comprehensively, considering not only their visual characteristics but also their interrelations. To demonstrate this capability, we extend the Existing Object-centric Scene Parsing (EOSSP) dataset to include transcripts of TV shows and generate image-question-answer triplets that focus on spatiotemporal relationships, requiring objects to be understood in context. Our findings show that our approach significantly improves scene understanding, with the dual-encoder model performing better than others even when using additional refinement modules. Additionally, it has been observed that our method can transfer knowledge more effectively to new scenarios than comparable models without the contrastive learning strategy.

A single, well-established benchmark offers the potential to link parton distribution functions and next-to-leading-order parton distribution function error estimates to various accelerator observables. This benchmark's accuracy can be used to evaluate the simulation settings for those same observables. This paper focuses on the benchmark of the transverse-momentum distribution in the lepton pairs observed at the Belle II detector, specifically those resulting from the decay of W bosons. It investigates how modifying the simulation settings affects this distribution and whether a single, well-defined adjustable parameter can accurately account for any variations in the lepton pairs' transverse-momentum distribution. The study also assesses whether this single adjustable parameter can be inferred from several other, simultaneously measured observables.

This study investigates the user experience of operating Telepresence Robots (TPRs) by conducting in-depth interviews with TPR users at three different locations. Our research revealed that users consider operational capabilities, such as navigation and system management, visual aspects, and the comfort level provided by the TPR to be equally significant. The results indicate that users rate these elements separately in terms of satisfaction and, according to the users' preferences, one area may influence the other while in operation. The data also suggests that users distinguish between the physical and visual aspects of the experience and that these elements may interrelate for some users although not for others. Based on our findings, we have developed guidelines for designing the user experience of TPRs, including incorporating user preferences into the device design, incorporating settings for adjusting the device's response to movements, and improving the device's visibility and comfort level.

Using a hierarchical statistical model, we analyze how the N1 plant's shoot height responds to varying soil nitrogen levels, and examine the effects of genetic factors on this relationship. To account for the correlated data, we establish a model where a random N1 effect is a drawing from a probability distribution that represents the impact of common environmental factors, in addition to true genetic factors. Utilizing an approach by Waddle et al., we incorporate the estimated parameters into a Bayesian hierarchical network to assess direct and indirect influences between variables. Through this analysis, we identify key variables with strong connections to N1 shoot height, and explore the potential for using these networks in exploring plant trait associations with environmental and genetic factors.

Mafia is a murder-mystery type party game that's been around since the 1930s, where a minority of'mafiosos' secretly scheme among the majority of 'inocents,' aiming to wipe out the other group, while special 'detectives' work to eliminate the mafia members, and the game has a vast array of variants that impact its dynamics, which are studied under a broad, abstract framework. A customized version of the game was developed with adjustable rules to fine-tune the game's characteristics, and since the game's behavior is highly influenced by a few key parameters, two-dimensional graphs were used to illustrate the game's outcomes and mafia growth based on these variables, which were found to be highly unpredictable due to the game's inherent complexity, resulting in a wide range of possible outcomes for any given set of parameters.

Planets of similar size to Earth's exoplanets are rare among observed stellar debris disks. Several stars hosting excess emission due to accretion of material from their disks are notable exceptions. We investigated two such stars, $\eta$ Tel and $\eta$ Ser, which are known to illuminate disks thought to be 10-15 million years old, and are now hosting planets. Simulations of accretion of material from the stars' disks reveal that it's feasible for multiple large planets to simultaneously form and grow in tandem, led by any of three processes: in situ accretion, migration followed by fast accretion, or merger of pre-planetary cores. Analyses of the stars' luminosity and orbital properties also indicate that their planets likely formed within a relatively short time frame, approximately 1-5 million years, which aligns with the age of the illuminated disks and the onset of intense disk migration. If these ages are accurate, it's possible that all three processes contributed to the formation of these planetary systems.

Our study examines the temperature-dependent electrical conductivity of armchair
single-wall carbon nanotubes grown on Au/Ni(111). A thin, uniform nanotube
film was analyzed using low-energy electron microscopy, low-energy electron
diffuse scattering, and x-ray photoemission spectroscopy. A wide range of energy
ranges from 0.4 to 6 eV was explored with low-energy electron transmission and
x-ray photoemission spectroscopy. We employed a Monte Carlo simulation to analyze
the electrical conductivity, which revealed that at high temperatures it is
primarily controlled by collisions between electrons and phonons. Nevertheless, a
distinct change in conductivity was observed at around 1000 K, which cannot be
explained solely by either electron-phonon or electron-electron collisions. We
attribute this change to a transition from high-temperature transport to
ballistic conduction. Additionally, our x-ray photoemission spectroscopy data
showed that both nanotube and gold surfaces exhibit similar Fermi level
distribution, with an energy offset of approximately 0.1 eV. An energy-dependent
electrical conductivity was observed, with ballistic conduction being more
noticable at higher energies.

A key challenge in fuzzy k-means clustering lies in balancing the protection of individual data points and the optimization of cluster assignments. To address this issue, we modify the objective function with entropy terms and incorporate a novel optimization technique based on the reparameterization trick in variational inference. This approach, which relies on stochastic gradient descent for end-to-end training, yields a competitive minimum, while our experimental results reveal a minimum close to the global optimum. Furthermore, we evaluate the robustness of our method against various forms of adversarial attacks and find that it successfully prevents extortion during the fuzzy k-means clustering process.

In dealing with intricate datasets that characters and graphs can represent, a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model has been utilized as an effective hidden unit system. Expert weights within the MoE model are adjusted through a process involving maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), typically utilizing a gradient descent (GD) method. Nevertheless, the standard MLE algorithm's reliance on complete observations may not suit situations involving partial access, common in complex datasets such as graphs, where only partial views of neighboring nodes are available. Furthermore, the conventional gradient descent method often leads to over-smoothing in more intricate tasks. To address these challenges, this paper introduces an alternate algorithm utilizing stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to refine the MoE model. Our proposed approach designates specific datasets for training solely the relevant expert nodes, thereby significantly decreasing overall training data requirements. Experimental evaluations on character and graph datasets demonstrate our model's superior performance when compared to conventional gradient-based methods in terms of forecasting accuracy and parameter estimation. Additionally, the work presents an analysis of learning patterns within stochastic gradient-based algorithms and provides an empirical examination of parameter distributions that have a considerable impact on forecasting.

This expository paper showcases the connection between the principles of Henry Clements' birational geometry framework and the more theoretical concepts of Jacobians, Prym varieties, and moduli spaces, highlighting their application in the context of unramified cohomology.

We develop a theoretical framework to analyze how gravitational forces break unitary global symmetries in particle physics models without the constraints of extra spatial dimensions. Our investigation encompasses various types of breaking, including complete and partial symmetry breakdown, involving defects like gravitational singularities and symholors. Under the assumption that graviton fields oscillate within the gravitational manifold, we calculate the magnitude of $\Delta W$ of the breaking in terms of Higgs field oscillation amplitude within the AdS space, yielding a bound of $\Delta W /f \lesssim 0.25$. This boundary has significant implications for theories of quantum gravity with compact or pathological gravitational manifolds, such as gravity-Higgs models, supergravity-Higgs models, linear dilaton gravity, and Liouville gravity, leading to substantial consequences for particle physics models. Furthermore, we extend the analysis to partial symmetry breaking within the context of global Galilean symmetries and particle physics models with Galilean-Higgs hairs. Our findings also encompass an in-depth discussion of ghost states arising from the linearization of Galilean symmetries.

Our investigation of the blue horizontal branch (BHB) of the globular cluster M30 begins by using the Gaia DR2 distance to the cluster, calculated as 3.88 plus or minus 0.11 parsecs. Through the Gaia DR2, we isolated distinct sub-populations within the BHB, denoted as BHBs1 and BHBs2, each of which exhibits uniform velocity space distribution. Utilizing half-light radius bounds derived from surface brightness fluctuations, we analyzed the color magnitudes of M30's stars and discovered that the redder BHBs1 population occupies the cluster's half-light radius, whereas the bluer BHBs2 population lies outside. The estimated ages for BHBs1 and BHBs2 are 7.3 plus or minus 0.4 and 9.5 plus or minus 0.4 billion years, respectively, based on Hertzprung-Helfelfinger diagrams, suggesting an approximately 2 billion year age difference. The relative frequencies and radial distributions of BHBs1 and BHBs2 indicate that the younger BHBs1 population resides closer to the cluster's center. However, both distributions are marked by an gradient. The difference in the shapes and characteristics of the gradients can be explained by the varying initial mass functions of BHBs1 and BHBs2, as a younger and more top-heavy IMF for BHBs1 contributing to a smoother distribution, whereas a more variable

The Madsen-Weiss theorem for integral Hachim maps, established in 2008, has far-reaching implications, including leading to the proof of the "b-principle" for morphisms, with associated stability theorems for maps and surfaces. Notably, this proof was long since realized by resolving the underlying hard topological issue, which was referred to as the "kinematic property" in the original proof. 

Building upon the recent breakthroughs by Galatius, Levine, and Miller on the kinematic property, we present a new approach centered around the modification of the Madsen-Weiss construction to focus on subintegral Hachim maps, along with detailed explicit cocycle definitions that illustrate its robustness. 

The presented method holds potential for direct generalization, thereby suggesting the extension of the Madsen-Weiss theorem to higher dimensional surfaces, which is currently under separate investigation by the authors.

The idea that deeper neural networks represent more complex information is contradicted by research demonstrating that even the least trainable lower layers of a model can recognize basic image features. Pretrained models employed for numerous visual tasks often fail similar tasks after being fine-tuned, despite outperforming other approaches. We attribute this failure to the loss of essential image features during the fine-tuning process. We propose a method to maintain the integrity of these features in the lower layers and prevent performance degradation. We showcase this method's effectiveness by surpassing the state-of-the-art in zero-shot object counting and achieving comparable results to leading methods, with the exception of surpassing the state-of-the-art in one instance. Additionally, we provide insights into the importance of distinguishing between individuals using image features, and how preserving these features can be beneficial in task success.

Networks with high modularity, meaning their communities are closely connected to each other while being isolated from outside nodes, are characteristic of many natural and man-made systems. In networks with high modularity, localized information tends to spread rapidly within each community before reaching the broader network. Researchers investigated how modularity impacts information spreading using a model based on simultaneous information diffusion in network communities. Networks were divided into communities, and each was an independent system with its own information spreading rate, and inter-community connections allowed exchange of active nodes. Networks were seeded with small groups of nodes, and the target was a smaller group of nodes. In networks characterized by high modularity, the optimal seed size for achieving the target outcome was found to be inversely related to both the seed and target sizes. In networks with low modularity, localized and inter-community information spreading occur simultaneously, and the optimal seed size varies based on the efficiencies of these processes. Networks with dual information spreading models allow for larger seed sizes or target criteria to be explored, and the authors examined both smaller seed sizes and larger targets, revealing a new rule of thumb that applies to many situations. These results were verified using both artificial and real-world networks with varying characteristics.

Research highlights the potential for a geometric Lagrangian angle defined on a special Lagrangian using its Cauchy-Grothendieck determinant, and investigates the determinant's properties. It demonstrates the determinant's continuity on special Lagrangians, with an angle that converges to 0 that implies Bruyere's conjecture. Additionally, evidence is provided that the determinant is nowhere singular. A previous finding that nowhere-singularity of the Bergman kernel for 2-dimensional Lagrangians is established, and it shows that the Bergman kernel's blow-up is controlled as Lagrangian angles converge to 0. This implies Bruyere's conjecture for special Lagrangians. Moreover, it is proven that special Lagrangian angles characterized by Lagrangian mean curvature operator converge to 0 as they vary within the homology group. This evidence is given for 2 and 5 dimensional Lagrangians. A non-bracket Lagrangian variant is also offered.

The majority of recent studies on generating discrete-time channel models have focused on scenarios where signals travel through amplified links. Conversely, fewer studies have been devoted to establishing reliable discrete-time channel models for unamplified links. This research aims to develop an underlying continuous-time channel model for unguided wireless links between satellite and ground stations, and to investigate the accuracy of a discrete-time channel model when it is approximated from this underlying model. Our findings reveal that the accuracy of the discrete-time channel model depends heavily on the type of modulation used, the elevation angle of the satellite, and the observed transmission duration. This research conducts experiments under non-ideal conditions, involving variations in temperature, elevation angles, and bandwidth. Utilizing data collected from actual measurements, we assess the effectiveness of the discrete-time channel model. Our results show that the discrete-time channel model can achieve an average symbol-error-rate of less than 0.10 for cases involving short-term fading, and that it accurately predicts an S-curve error of less than 2% when it is applied to new sets of transmission parameters that were not used in its original creation. This research's findings are similar to those obtained in prior studies for amplified fiber-optic channels. This research aims to contribute knowledge by providing insights that are relevant to designing reliable communication systems.

Feely et al.'s (2022) categorization of problem-space evasion attacks is the most comprehensive classification system to date, encompassing 12 different types of attacks. However, a close examination by our research team reveals that these categories are subject to ambiguities in interpretation, potentially leading to inconsistent application in real-world scenarios. Consequently, we develop a more refined taxonomy with enhanced specificity, incorporating Feely et al.'s categories and adding distinct subcategories for each evasion strategy. The new taxonomy is systematically analyzed using Chao Liu's (2022) evaluation framework for classification systems, resulting in two major branches: Evading via Modifying Features and Evading via Selecting Features. Each of these branches is further subdivided into more precise subcategories, ultimately totaling eleven distinct types of problem-space evasion attacks. This more fine-tuned taxonomy enables researchers and practitioners to evaluate and compare existing classifications in Chao Liu's (2022) framework, while also providing a clearer understanding of each evasion strategy for classifying problem-space attacks.

A key benefit of cloud-based services is the ability to manage them orchestrally, yet numerous service providers continue to utilize traditional methods for managing containers. This paper introduces Ozy, a complete containerization system that promises increased resource utilization and is straightforward to use. Ozy achieves these benefits via a streamlined installation process, user-friendly management features, and efficient, multi-service container scheduling. To test and validate Ozy, the authors designed a trial application for monitoring the local network and assessing energy consumption. As part of this trial, the authors collaborated with an industrial partner, OzyTech, to put Ozy to the test in real-world settings.

The one-dimensional fractional quantum Hall system exhibits a diverse spectrum of incompressible phases originating from the Laughlin states, characterized by unique filling factors of the form $\frac{1}{2s}$, where $s$ is an odd integer. Recent numerical investigations have revealed that the phase associated with $s=3$ can re-enter the previously documented phases associated with $s=2$ when an additional electron is added. This re-entry is distinct from the known re-entrance of the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian phases, caused by a change in the Moore-Read ground state's topological order from 10 to 8. An analytical approach aims to establish that the phase associated with $s=3$ shares certain unconventional properties, specifically a larger ground state degeneracy and non-Abelian, gauge-fixed degenerate states near half-filling that are symmetrical under electron-hole exchanges. This distinct character separates the $s=3$ phase from both the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian phases, identifying it as a unique "anomalous quantized phase".

Researchers initially assumed that the Thakurur metric, with its singularities, was the only possible representation of the metric in question. However, it has been discovered that this assumption is not valid when analyzing high-density primordial black holes. A new, non-singular representation of the Thakurur metric has been found and been used to revisit constraints on the Thakurur metric, which relates to the amount of primordial black holes in the universe. Surprisingly, even with the alternative representation in use, current restrictions on primordial black holes remain effective. This new representation may have useful applications in analyzing more complex spacetimes, such as those related to charged black holes.

The process of core growth within a protoplanetary disc is enhanced when dust particles are trapped in ring-like structures that emerge due to the dynamics of the disc's shear instability. This ring-like pattern not only amplifies the dust particles' density and their ability to grow into larger particles, but also reduces the rate at which they are transported towards the star. Our investigations focus on the disc areas where core growth can occur, by analyzing the effects of dust particles on the radial movement of particles within these dust rings, for both long-lived rings in critical equilibrium and shorter-lived rings in non-equilibrium that are seen in simulations. Our results show that in these non-equilibrium rings, the rate of radial movement is significantly reduced by factors of 2-3, when compared to a simple model that assumes particles are uniformly distributed, this implies that growth into large particles can occur within these non-equitable structures, even at lower disc masses, when compared to a simple model that assumes particles are uniformly distributed, and core growth can occur within these structures, even at lower disc masses.

Deep learning techniques often rely on empirical risk minimization, but this approach provides minimal insight into the underlying dynamics of their behavior.  We investigate an alternative method, robust learning, which delivers universally strong bounds for neural network training dynamics.  By utilizing a non-linear spectral decomposition, this approach yields model-independent bounds applicable to both linear and non-linear systems.  Although our bounds are somewhat conservative, they demonstrate a significant improvement over previous results for model-dependent bounds.  Interestingly, robust learning often requires fewer model parameters than non-robust learning, with adjustments varying from mild for simple models to highly severe for complex models.  Moreover, robust learning's need for parameters can be alleviated as $n\rightarrow\infty$.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by achieving precise dynamic patterns on a variety of toy models with a minimal number of parameters.  Finally, we utilize our approach to study the dynamic behavior of a model that effectively learns the MNIST dataset.

Consider two subgroups, M and N, of a countable abelian group G, and let A and B be subsets of M and N, respectively, that also consist of elements from G. The question of existence of Bohr sets in sumsets A + B is explored within the context of subgroups M and N of G. It's proven that for sumsets A + B, the upper Banach density of which exceeds a certain threshold, the existence of Bohr sets is established. This result not only generalizes previous findings but also answers a query raised by the paper by the correspondents Kolgatin and Petrich. Moreover, it's been shown that for almost all subsets of M and N, with Banach upper density close to a certain value, the existence of Bohr sets is established. Specifically, it's been shown that for almost all subsets of M and N, with Banach upper density greater than a certain value, defined as the maximum of 1/2 and 1/π and denoted by ρ, the existence of Bohr sets is established. This has led to the discovery that for subgroups M and N of G, with Banach upper density of M greater than ρ and almost all subsets of N, with Banach upper density greater than ρ, the existence of right ideal sums of M and N, within the context of right ideals of the groupoid M ⊸N, has been established.

A common strategy to decrease energy consumption and lower emissions in moving people and goods is to schedule transportation efficiently. To accomplish this, optimization problems must be solved, and it is possible that not all available routes can be utilized due to constraints. Typically, solving these optimization problems is a challenging task as it involves vast amounts of data. Research has shown that contributing path information can greatly aid in solving these optimization problems. Nevertheless, in real-world conditions, moving vehicles cannot always adhere to predetermined paths due to various obstacles. To address this limitation, this study develops an algorithm that utilizes an online planning technique based on stochastic programming. The aim of this algorithm is to identify an efficient travel schedule that is similar to the optimal solution and also takes into account real-time disruptions. The study evaluates its performance through simulations with various levels of uncertainty and disruption. The results demonstrate that this approach can achieve a good travel schedule while keeping track of changes and handling uncertainty. Furthermore, this technique is versatile and can be applied to various transportation problems, such as those related to heavy industry, with potential extensions to other applications.

This study investigates the resilience of visual systems in the face of unprecedented events. To enhance preparedness, it's crucial to incorporate various information sources, including text, knowledge, and experience. Although single modalities can provide context, they often perform better when multiple sources of information are combined. Nevertheless, missing or contradictory data in multiple modalities can greatly impact a system's performance. To address these challenges, we specifically investigate the robustness and adaptability of visual systems in complex environments. Firstly, we establish a framework for handling diverse modalities that utilizes text, knowledge, experience, and visual data. Using a unified approach, we specifically vary the sources of information to test the system's preparedness and adaptability. Using a state-of-the-art model, we evaluate the system's performance in unexpected situations, including novel object classes, scenarios, and contexts. While it's challenging to predict the outcome of real-world events, our findings indicate that systems designed to draw on multiple information sources can greatly improve their preparedness and adaptability in complex environments. More importantly, we specifically demonstrate the efficacy of incorporating prior knowledge in enhancing the system's robustness and practical applications. This research opens up an important area of study, inviting the machine learning and computer vision communities to share knowledge and expand the range of human vision and knowledge. The study's findings are available online at http://github.com/asharakeh/robust-visual-systems.

Research aims to find early Alzheimer's disease using machine learning techniques, typically trained on labeled data. However, labeling is costly due to the need for MRI interpretation by experts, limiting the size of available datasets for training supervised models. We investigate whether unsupervised learning can effectively identify Alzheimer's disease from large, expert-labeled datasets, and compare its performance to supervised convolutional neural networks. We develop an unsupervised method that uses change-based representation to classify three stages of brain disease progression. The approach yields comparable results to supervised models to identify individuals with Alzheimer's disease who have progressed to a certain stage, exhibiting promising cross-validation and actual predictions on an independent dataset. Despite achieving similar classification accuracy, the unsupervised method offers the advantage of allowing the reuse of trained models without requiring access to expert-labeled data for subsequent applications. Moreover, the unsupervised method demonstrates the potential to identify individuals at an early stage of disease progression, albeit not as effectively as supervised models trained on disease progression labels.

The Backward Dropping Algorithm serves as an efficient method for data reduction, addressing issues of temporal complexity and mitigating the effects of long-term dependencies in datasets.
